blocks.title: NaN pitfall:
blocks.text: `NaN == NaN` is **False**, so `discount == np.nan` finds nothing. Always test gaps with `isna()`.

blocks.title: Key takeaways:
blocks.text: `isna().sum()` counts gaps. `fillna` returns a ==copy==. `dropna(subset=)` drops rows. `mean` **skips** NaN.

blocks.title: Key takeaways:
blocks.text: `pivot_table` aggregates and fills gaps; `margins=True` adds **All**. `groupby` + `unstack` gives the same table. `melt` goes wide to long and keeps NaN. `crosstab` counts combinations.

blocks.title: Speed rule:
blocks.text: A boolean mask sums to a count. Reach for `between`, `isin` and `np.where` before writing `apply(axis=1)`.

blocks.title: Key takeaways:
blocks.text: Use ==vectorised== column maths first. `map`, `np.where` and `pd.cut` cover most recodes, so keep `apply(axis=1)` for the rare case.

caption.text:
50 pandas drills to crack any data interview.

Fifty hands-on exercises, every one with an answer, all run against one small sales, products, stores and customers dataset. Learn the data once and spend your time on the pandas.

What the drills cover, in order:

• Selection and Filtering
• Missing Data
• Merge and Join
• GroupBy and Agg
• Pivot and Melt
• Apply vs Vectorised
• Datetime Handling
• Window and Rolling
• Real Analyst Scenarios

They build from the basics up to the kind of scenarios analysts get handed on the job, with a cheatsheet at the end to revise from.

Save this for your next interview prep session and send it to the friend who keeps saying they'll practise pandas.

Comment “pandas” to get every query and answer as a PDF.
